Reese Witherspoon says she wants to banish the myth that young women are not at risk for breast cancer. (CNN) -- Every three minutes in the United States, a woman is diagnosed with breast cancer. As a woman, a mother, and a daughter, I find that statistic terrifying. I was never naïve about breast cancer, but hearing this statistic put it all into perspective. But the moment I heard "every three minutes," I felt vulnerable and scared as I realized that anyone is susceptible. The only way for me to ease my fears was to take action. I had access to an entire organization that is dedicated to giving back to women and educating people. So I started asking, "What do I need to know?" It was through that curiosity that I found out the most important fact in breast cancer: Early detection saves lives. According to the Avon Foundation Breast Cancer Crusade, there is a 97 percent five-year survival rate when breast cancer is caught before it spreads to other parts of the body. When breast cancer first develops, there are usually no symptoms, which is why women need to perform self-exams regularly and contact their doctor upon noticing even the smallest change. Of course talking about breast cancer and breast health is a personal thing. I too am a private person but encourage all women to break through their reservations and talk to their doctors and physicians. We must also banish the myth that young women are not at risk for breast cancer. At the Avon Walk in Washington, I met young survivors who were diagnosed in their 20s, an age when most women are graduating from college and just starting their lives as full adults.  Watch Reese and Larry at the Avon Walk » . Women in their 20s and 30s should have a clinical breast exam by a health professional at least once every three years and women 40 and older should have an exam every year. I am passionate about fighting this devastating disease. I fight for my mother, myself, my children and future generations of women, so one day we will not have to be afraid of breast cancer. I began my fight by learning important first steps in breast cancer detection, and will not end my fight until every woman can stand together saying we are breast cancer free. More than anything else, I have faith -- faith we will find a cure. I saw this commitment in the faces of the women in Washington -- in the faces of the women walking and the women and men who stood on the sidelines encouraging the 3,500 participants to the finish line. I was cheering right along with them, screaming for action to find a cure.  Avon's next walk will take place in New York City on October 4 and 5.

**Editor’s Note:** Reese Witherspoon, the Academy Award-winning actress, serves as honorary chair of the Avon Foundation and is employed by Avon Products as its global ambassador.

Reese Witherspoon says she wants to dispel the myth that young women are not at risk for breast cancer.

Women close to me have battled the disease and are now soldiers in the broader fight against it. But the moment I heard “every three minutes,” I felt vulnerable and afraid, realizing that anyone can be susceptible. The only way to ease my fears was to take action. I needed to educate myself and others about this disease.

As Honorary Chair of the Avon Foundation, I had valuable resources at my fingertips. I had access to an entire organization dedicated to giving back to women and educating the public. So I began asking, “What do I need to know?”

Through that curiosity, I learned the most important fact about breast cancer: early detection saves lives. According to the Avon Foundation Breast Cancer Crusade, there is a 97 percent five-year survival rate when breast cancer is detected before it spreads to other parts of the body.

When breast cancer first develops, there are usually no symptoms, which is why women need to perform self-exams regularly and contact their doctor upon noticing even the smallest change.

Of course, talking about breast cancer and breast health is deeply personal. I, too, am a private person, but I encourage all women to overcome their reservations and speak with their doctors and physicians. We must also dispel the myth that young women are not at risk for breast cancer.

At the Avon Walk in Washington, I met young survivors who were diagnosed in their 20s—an age when most women are graduating from college and just beginning their lives as adults.

Watch Reese and Larry at the Avon Walk »

Women in their 20s and 30s should have a clinical breast exam by a health professional at least once every three years, and women 40 and older should have an exam every year.

I am passionate about fighting this devastating disease. I fight for my mother, myself, my children, and future generations of women, so that one day we will no longer have to fear breast cancer. I began my fight by learning the essential first steps in breast cancer detection, and I will not end that fight until every woman can stand together and say we are breast cancer-free.

Editor’s Note: Reese Witherspoon, an Academy Award-winning actress, serves as honorary chair of the Avon Foundation and works with Avon Products as its global ambassador. She says she hopes to dispel the false belief that young women do not face a risk of breast cancer.

(CNN) -- In the United States, a woman receives a breast cancer diagnosis every three minutes. As a woman, a mother, and a daughter, I find that number deeply frightening. I was never unaware of the seriousness of breast cancer, but that statistic made the danger feel much more real.

Women I care about have faced this illness and have become fighters in the broader battle against it. Still, when I heard the words “every three minutes,” I felt exposed and afraid, understanding in a new way that no one is immune. The only thing that helped calm that fear was deciding to act. I knew I had to learn more about the disease and help others learn as well.

As honorary chair of the Avon Foundation, I had valuable tools and information available to me. I was connected to an entire organization devoted to supporting women and educating the public. So I began by asking, “What do I need to understand?”

That desire to learn led me to the most crucial truth about breast cancer: finding it early can save lives. The Avon Foundation Breast Cancer Crusade reports that when breast cancer is detected before it has spread elsewhere in the body, the five-year survival rate is 97 percent.

In its earliest stages, breast cancer often causes no noticeable symptoms. That is why women should examine themselves regularly and call their doctor if they notice even the smallest change.

Talking about breast cancer and breast health can feel very personal. I am a private person too, but I urge women to move past hesitation and have these conversations with their doctors and health care providers.

We also have to eliminate the misconception that young women are safe from breast cancer. At the Avon Walk in Washington, I met young survivors who had been diagnosed while still in their 20s — a time when many women are finishing college and beginning adult life.

Watch Reese and Larry at the Avon Walk »

Women in their 20s and 30s should receive a clinical breast exam from a health professional at least once every three years. Women age 40 and older should have one every year.

I am deeply committed to battling this devastating disease. I fight for my mother, for myself, for my children, and for future generations of women, with the hope that someday breast cancer will no longer be something we fear.

My own fight began with learning the basic, essential steps for detecting breast cancer early. I will not stop fighting until all women can stand together and say that we are free from breast cancer.

Above all, I have faith — faith that a cure will be found. I saw that determination in Washington, in the faces of the women walking and in the women and men along the route who encouraged all 3,500 participants to reach the finish line.

I was cheering with them, calling for action and for a cure.

Avon’s next walk is scheduled for October 4 and 5 in New York City.

## Opinion: Breast cancer awareness is not just a month. It is a lifeline.

Every October, we see pink ribbons on lapels, storefronts and football fields. We hear the familiar calls for awareness. We are reminded to honor survivors, remember those we have lost and support the people still facing a diagnosis that can change a life in an instant.

But breast cancer awareness cannot be something we put on the calendar and then set aside. Awareness matters most when it becomes action — when it leads someone to schedule a mammogram, ask about family history, notice a change in their body or help a loved one get the care they need.

Breast cancer is deeply personal for millions of families. It affects mothers, daughters, sisters, friends, coworkers and neighbors. It can arrive with fear and confusion, but it can also be met with knowledge, community and lifesaving medical care. That is why early detection is so important.

When breast cancer is found early, treatment is often more effective. Screening does not eliminate the fear of cancer, but it can give women and their doctors more options. Mammograms, clinical exams and conversations with health care providers are not just medical appointments — they are acts of self-protection.

Still, too many women face barriers to getting screened. Some do not have insurance. Some live far from clinics. Some are juggling work, childcare and caregiving responsibilities. Some are afraid of what they might find. And some have not been given clear information about when to begin screening or what symptoms to take seriously.

That is where public awareness must meet public commitment.

Through my work with the Avon Foundation, I saw the power of bringing women together around a shared purpose: funding research, expanding access to care, supporting education and making sure breast cancer is not treated as a private burden women must carry alone. The Foundation’s efforts helped shine a light on the importance of early detection and the need to reach women wherever they are — in their communities, workplaces, churches and homes.

Awareness campaigns work best when they are rooted in compassion and practicality. It is not enough to tell women to “get checked” if they cannot afford the appointment. It is not enough to celebrate survivors without fighting for better outcomes for everyone. It is not enough to wear pink without asking whether women in underserved communities have the same chance at early diagnosis and quality treatment.

Breast cancer does not affect all women equally. Black women in the United States, for example, are more likely to die from breast cancer than white women, even though incidence rates are similar. That disparity should be unacceptable to all of us. It speaks to gaps in access, treatment, trust and timely care — and it demands action from health systems, policymakers, advocates and communities.

We also need to broaden the conversation. Breast cancer awareness should include younger women learning what is normal for their bodies. It should include men, who can also develop breast cancer and who play an important role in supporting the women in their lives. It should include families talking honestly about medical history. And it should include survivors whose experiences do not end when treatment does.

For many people, breast cancer leaves physical and emotional scars long after the last appointment. Survivorship can bring relief, gratitude, anxiety and exhaustion all at once. We owe survivors more than applause. We owe them continued support, better follow-up care, workplace understanding and a culture that listens to their full stories.

The message I hope every woman hears is simple: Your health matters. Your questions matter. Your instincts about your body matter. If something feels different, say something. If you are due for a screening, make the appointment. If you are scared, ask someone to go with you. And if you have already been through breast cancer, know that your courage helps light the way for someone else.

This work belongs to all of us. Companies can fund research and screening programs. Lawmakers can protect access to preventive care. Doctors can communicate clearly and respectfully. Friends can remind friends to make appointments. Families can talk openly about risk. And each of us can help replace fear and stigma with information and support.

Pink ribbons are a symbol. But the real power is in what we do after we see them.

Breast cancer awareness is not just about hope. It is about action — early detection, equal access, better treatment and a future where more women live long, healthy lives after diagnosis.

That is a future worth fighting for.

## Why Young Women Shouldn’t Ignore Breast Cancer Risk

When you’re young, it’s easy to think breast cancer is something to worry about later. Life is busy—school, work, relationships, family, friendships, building a future. Health concerns can get pushed to the bottom of the list, especially when you feel perfectly fine.

But breast cancer risk is not something young women should ignore.

While breast cancer is more common as women get older, younger women can and do get diagnosed. And when breast cancer occurs in younger women, it may sometimes be found at a later stage because people assume they are “too young” for it to happen. That’s why awareness, regular checkups, and knowing your own body matter so much.

Taking care of your breast health is not about living in fear. It’s about being informed, confident, and proactive.

### Know What’s Normal for You

One of the most important things young women can do is become familiar with how their breasts normally look and feel. Breasts can change throughout the menstrual cycle, with pregnancy, breastfeeding, weight changes, medications, and aging. Many changes are not cancer—but knowing your normal makes it easier to notice when something feels different.

Pay attention to changes such as:

- A new lump or thickened area  
- Swelling or changes in breast shape  
- Skin dimpling or puckering  
- Nipple discharge, especially if bloody or spontaneous  
- Nipple pulling inward  
- Redness, warmth, or persistent rash  
- Ongoing pain in one specific area  

If you notice something unusual, don’t panic—but don’t ignore it either. Make an appointment with a healthcare professional and get it checked.

### Family History Matters—But It Isn’t Everything

Some young women are at higher risk because of family history or inherited genetic mutations such as BRCA1 or BRCA2. If your mother, sister, grandmother, aunt, or other close relatives have had breast or ovarian cancer—especially at a young age—it’s worth discussing with your doctor.

But it’s also important to know this: many people diagnosed with breast cancer do not have a strong family history. So even if breast cancer doesn’t “run in your family,” breast awareness is still important.

### Regular Exams Are an Act of Self-Respect

A clinical breast exam during a routine healthcare visit can be an important part of preventive care, especially if you have symptoms or elevated risk. Your healthcare provider can help you understand what screenings are appropriate for your age, personal history, and risk level.

For many women, routine mammograms begin later in adulthood, but some may need earlier screening if they have higher risk factors. That’s why a personalized conversation with a doctor is so valuable.

Don’t be afraid to ask:

- When should I start breast cancer screening?
- Do I have risk factors that mean I should be screened earlier?
- Should I consider genetic counseling or testing?
- What changes should I watch for?
- How often should I have a clinical breast exam?

These are smart questions. They are not overreactions.

### Don’t Let Embarrassment or Fear Stop You

It can feel awkward to talk about breast changes. It can feel scary to make the appointment. Many women delay care because they don’t want to seem dramatic, or they’re worried about what they might find out.

But here’s the truth: getting checked is powerful.

Most breast changes are not cancer. And if something does need attention, finding it earlier can make a real difference. You deserve answers. You deserve care. You deserve to be taken seriously.

### Encourage the Women Around You

Breast health shouldn’t be a whispered conversation. Talk to your friends. Remind your sister to schedule her appointment. Ask your mom about family medical history. Share information without shame or fear.

Sometimes the encouragement one woman gives another is the nudge that leads to an important doctor’s visit.

### Take Care of Yourself—Now, Not Someday

Young women are often taught to take care of everyone else first. But your health belongs on the list too. Regular exams, body awareness, and honest conversations with healthcare providers are simple but meaningful steps.

You don’t need to be anxious. You don’t need to obsess. You just need to pay attention.

Breast cancer awareness is not only for later in life. It’s for every woman who wants to protect her future, trust her instincts, and treat her body with the care it deserves.

So schedule the appointment. Ask the question. Notice the change. Encourage a friend.

Your health is worth your time.

**Opinion: Walking for the women we love — and for the lives we can still save**  
*By [Celebrity Name]*

I have walked red carpets, stages and film sets. But some of the most meaningful steps I’ve ever taken have been alongside women in pink — survivors, daughters, sisters, mothers, friends — during the Avon Walk for Breast Cancer.

Anyone who has participated in an event like the Avon Walk knows it is more than a fundraiser. It is a moving portrait of courage. You see women who have endured chemotherapy and surgery. You see families carrying photos of loved ones who should still be here. You see strangers become a community because cancer has a way of reminding us how deeply connected we are.

Breast cancer is not an abstract issue. It is one of the most common cancers affecting women in the United States. About 1 in 8 women will be diagnosed with invasive breast cancer in her lifetime. Those numbers are frightening — but they do not tell the whole story.

Here is the part we must talk about more: early detection saves lives.

According to widely cited cancer survival data, when breast cancer is found early, before it has spread beyond the breast, the five-year relative survival rate is about 99%. When it has spread to nearby lymph nodes, survival remains significantly higher than when the disease is found after it has metastasized to distant parts of the body. Once breast cancer is diagnosed at a distant stage, the five-year survival rate drops dramatically.

Behind every percentage point is a person. A woman who gets to attend her child’s graduation. A grandmother who gets more birthdays. A friend who gets to heal, rebuild and live.

That is why awareness cannot stop at wearing pink in October. Awareness must become education. Education must become action.

Women need clear, accessible information about their own bodies: what changes to look for, when to speak up, how to understand their personal risk and when to begin screening. Mammograms are not perfect, but they remain one of the most important tools we have for detecting breast cancer early. Clinical guidance can vary depending on age, family history, genetic risk and other factors, so every woman deserves a conversation with a trusted health care provider about what screening plan is right for her.

But education is not enough if access is unequal.

Too many women delay care because they are uninsured or underinsured. Too many cannot take time off work. Too many live far from screening centers. Too many are told, directly or indirectly, that their pain, fear or questions can wait. And we know that breast cancer outcomes are not the same for everyone. Black women in the United States are more likely to die from breast cancer than White women, despite similar or sometimes lower incidence rates. That gap is not about biology alone; it reflects disparities in access, timely diagnosis, quality treatment and systemic inequities that must be addressed.

This is why walks, campaigns and community events matter. The Avon Walk helped raise funds and visibility for breast cancer programs, research and support services. But perhaps just as importantly, it gave people a place to tell the truth: that cancer is terrifying, that survival is possible, and that no one should have to navigate diagnosis alone.

I have met survivors who found a lump during a self-exam and insisted on being seen. I have met women who nearly skipped a mammogram because life was too busy — and later said that appointment saved them. I have met families who turned grief into advocacy so another woman might get screened sooner.

Their message is simple: Pay attention. Ask questions. Do not ignore changes. Do not let fear keep you from a doctor’s office.

Early detection does not guarantee an easy road, and it does not prevent every loss. Breast cancer is complex, and metastatic disease still takes far too many lives. We must continue investing in research, better treatments and support for patients at every stage — especially those living with advanced breast cancer, whose voices deserve to be central in this conversation.

But we should also be honest about the power we already have. We can educate. We can screen. We can reduce barriers. We can normalize conversations about breast health in families, workplaces, churches, schools and communities. We can make sure women know that noticing a change in their breast is not “overreacting.” It is self-protection.

So today, I am thinking of every woman who has walked through diagnosis with grace she never should have had to summon. I am thinking of the loved ones we have lost. I am thinking of the doctors, nurses, researchers, advocates and volunteers who keep showing up. And I am thinking of the woman who is reading this and realizing she has been putting off an appointment.

Please make the call.

Schedule the screening. Ask about your risk. Encourage the women you love to do the same. If something feels wrong, say something. If you are dismissed, ask again. Your life is worth persistence.

The Avon Walk taught me that every step matters. In the fight against breast cancer, so does every conversation, every mammogram, every act of education and every woman who learns that her health is not something to postpone.

We walk for the survivors. We walk for the ones we miss. And we walk toward a future where more women are diagnosed early, treated fairly and given the chance to live full, beautiful lives.

## Turning Fear Into Action

When I first began working with the Avon Foundation, I was struck by something I have never forgotten: breast cancer is not an abstract issue. It is personal. It is a mother, a sister, a daughter, a best friend, a neighbor. It is someone sitting at a kitchen table trying to make sense of a diagnosis, someone lying awake at night wondering what comes next, someone finding courage she did not know she had.

As honorary chair of the Avon Foundation, I have met women whose lives have been changed by breast cancer, and I have been deeply moved by their honesty, strength, and resilience. I have heard stories of fear—real fear. Fear of the unknown. Fear of treatment. Fear of leaving family behind. Fear of not being able to afford care. Fear of hearing the words no one wants to hear.

But I have also seen what happens when fear is met with action.

Action can begin with a conversation. It can be a reminder to schedule a mammogram, a ride to a doctor’s appointment, a donation to research, a call to a friend who is going through treatment, or a decision to speak openly so another woman feels less alone. Action can be as simple as saying, “I’m here,” and meaning it.

One of the most powerful lessons I have learned is that hope is not passive. Hope is something we build. We build it through research. We build it through early detection. We build it through access to quality care for every woman, regardless of where she lives or how much money she has. We build it by standing together and refusing to accept that any woman should face breast cancer without support.

The Avon Foundation’s work matters because it reaches women where they are. It helps fund education, screening, treatment access, and scientific research. It recognizes that saving lives is not only about what happens in a laboratory, though research is essential. It is also about making sure women have information, resources, and a community around them when they need it most.

I believe in the possibility of a cure. I believe in the researchers who dedicate their lives to finding better treatments. I believe in the doctors, nurses, advocates, caregivers, and survivors who show us every day what courage looks like. And I believe that every step we take—every dollar raised, every woman screened, every voice lifted—moves us closer to the day when breast cancer no longer takes the people we love.

Fear is real. But fear does not get the final word.

Action does.

And with action, there is hope—hope for earlier detection, hope for better treatment, hope for longer lives, and hope for a cure.

That is why I am proud to stand with the Avon Foundation and with all the women and families affected by breast cancer. Together, we can turn concern into commitment, awareness into progress, and hope into something powerful enough to change lives.
